sections.text: Your fixed monthly payment is the one number M that, paid n times, exactly repays a balance P charged interest at a monthly rate r. The formula is M = P x r(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1). This article derives it from a one-line idea, runs it on a $300,000 loan, and shows which input moves the payment most. The question here is where the formula comes from and how sensitive it is, not how to read a schedule.
Deriving the formula in four lines
Start with how a balance evolves. Each month interest of r times the balance is added, then you pay M. After payment k the balance is B(k) = B(k-1) x (1+r) - M, with B(0) = P.

items: Unroll the recursion n times: B(n) = P(1+r)^n - M x [(1+r)^(n-1) + ... + (1+r) + 1].
The bracket is a geometric series with sum ((1+r)^n - 1) / r.
A loan that is fully repaid has B(n) = 0, so P(1+r)^n = M x ((1+r)^n - 1) / r.
Solve for M: M = P x r(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1). Dividing top and bottom by (1+r)^n gives the equivalent form M = P x r / (1 - (1+r)^-n).

sections.text: If the rate is zero the formula divides zero by zero, and the payment is simply P / n: $300,000 over 360 months is $833.33.
A full calculation, $300,000 at 6% for 30 years
Assumptions: annual rate 6%, so r = 0.06 / 12 = 0.005; term 30 years, so n = 360; payments at the end of each month.

items: Rule of thumb that follows: each $1,000 borrowed at 6% over 30 years costs $5.9955 a month.

sections.text: Check against the schedule: month 1 interest is $300,000 x 0.005 = $1,500.00, so $298.65 reduces the balance to $299,701.35. Month 2 interest is $1,498.51 and principal $300.14. Carrying this to payment 360 brings the balance to zero. Total paid is about $647,514.57 and total interest about $347,514.57. A lender rounds the payment to the cent, so the last payment differs from the others by a few cents, and the totals above use the unrounded payment, as the amortization calculator does.

To see the mechanics without a calculator, borrow $1,000 at 12% a year (r = 1% a month) for 3 months. The formula gives M = 1,000 x 0.01 x 1.01^3 / (1.01^3 - 1) = $340.02. Month 1: interest $10.00, principal $330.02, balance $669.98. Month 2: interest $6.70, principal $333.32, balance $336.66. Month 3: interest $3.37, principal $336.66, balance $0.00. Each payment is identical, the interest shrinks as the balance shrinks, and the balance lands on zero exactly because M was derived to make that happen.

The same equation answers other questions if you rearrange it. Loan size from a payment: P = M x (1 - (1+r)^-n) / r. At 6% over 30 years, a $1,500 monthly payment supports a loan of about $250,187 and a $2,000 payment supports about $333,583. Payoff time from a payment: n = -ln(1 - P x r / M) / ln(1+r). Paying $1,900 a month on the $300,000 loan instead of $1,798.65 gives n of about 312 payments, roughly 26 years, which is how extra payments shorten a loan.
Which input moves the payment most?

Payment is exactly proportional to the loan amount: a $150,000 loan at 6% over 30 years has a $899.33 payment, half of $1,798.65. The rate and the term are not proportional. Holding $300,000 and 30 years, changing the rate gives:
Going from 4% to 8% raises the payment by 53.7% ($1,432.25 to $2,201.29), while total interest rises 2.28 times. Now hold 6% and change the term:

Stretching from 15 to 30 years cuts the payment from $2,531.57 to $1,798.65 but more than doubles the interest, from $155,682.69 to $347,514.57. The lower payment is paid for with years of extra interest.

items: Plugging in the annual rate: r must be the periodic rate, the annual rate divided by 12 for monthly payments.
Mixing units: n counts payments, so a 30-year loan is 360, not 30.
Forgetting what the payment excludes: a mortgage bill may also include property tax, insurance or mortgage insurance, which are not part of M.

Expecting it to fit every loan: the formula assumes a fixed rate, equal payments and a monthly period. Adjustable-rate loans recompute it each time the rate changes, and loans that accrue interest daily or have fees will differ slightly.
Treating the first-year payment split as typical: the formula fixes M, but interest and principal inside M change every month.

sections.text: All figures are illustrative calculations using stated assumptions, not a loan offer. Your lender's disclosure is the authority for your actual payment.
